claims.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys can exhibit dual-phase lamellar microstructures containing many internal phase boundaries.
Internal lamellar boundaries act as microcrack-initiation sites and lead to brittle failure during room-temperature tensile deformation.
The proposed intervention combines addition of a controlled amount of a selected dopant with a brief post-doping anneal.
A short anneal after doping will cause the dopant to segregate preferentially to lamellar interfaces.
Dopant segregation will form coherent, nanoscale, ductile interfacial films along lamellar boundaries.
Nanoscale solute-segregation zones can occur near phase boundaries in a eutectic dual-phase high-entropy alloy without forming complex intermetallic compounds.
Segregation-modified interfaces will have enhanced interfacial cohesion.
The proposed interfacial films will reduce local stress concentrations.
The proposed interfacial films will suppress microcrack initiation and propagation.
Engineered interfacial chemistry will enhance dislocation transmission across lamellar interfaces.
The treatment will preserve a high-strength bulk microstructure.
The doped and annealed alloy will show simultaneous increases in tensile strength and room-temperature elongation relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline.
Complex intermetallic secondary phases can be intrinsically brittle and produce stress concentrations.
The predicted improvement is conditional on forming nanoscale segregated interfaces without larger secondary phases or embrittled interfacial regions.
Excessive dopant concentrations or incorrect annealing parameters may generate undesirable phases.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant simultaneous increase in strength and ductility, or failure to detect the proposed coherent nanoscale film, would falsify the hypothesis.
